Page 2 of 16 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:25:13 +0530 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Sh. Mohd. Tufail (hereinafter referred to as "the Complainant") against Sh. Arvind Kumar Jha (hereinafter referred to as "the Accused") under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant and accused persons were neighbours and accused No.1 represented himself to be the owner of property bearing Nos. 240 and 263, Ali Village, Sarita Vihar, New Delhi, measuring approximately 50 square yards out of Khasra No.101, and expressed his willingness to sell the said property to the complainant. That, an oral agreement to sell was entered into between the parties in the presence of independent witnesses for total sale consideration of Rs.24,00,000/-, out of which the complainant paid Rs.22,00,000/- as earnest money in cash on 08.10.2013. That, at the time of receiving the said amount, the accused handed over the original title documents of the property to the complainant and assured that the property would be transferred in favour of the complainant within fifteen days. That, the complainant kept approaching the accused for execution of the necessary documents, but the accused kept avoiding the matter on one pretext or another. That, subsequently, Accused No.1 expressed his inability to complete the transaction on the ground that Accused No.2, his wife, was unwilling to sell the property and CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 3 of 16 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:25:18 +0530 requested cancellation of the oral agreement. That, accused no. 1 to discharge his liability issued Cheque No.141711 dated 10.11.2013 for Rs.22,00,000/-, drawn on Punjab National Bank, Sarita Vihar Branch, New Delhi, in favour of the complainant. B. That, believing the assurances of the accused, the complainant presented the cheque on 28.12.2013 through his bank i.e. Corporation Bank, Ali Village, New Delhi. However, the cheque was dishonoured and returned unpaid on 30.12.2013 with the remarks "Funds Insufficient". That, on the insistence of accused, the complainant again presented the cheque on 11.01.2014, but the cheque was once again dishonoured on 15.01.2014 for the reason "Funds Insufficient". C. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through his counsel, dated 05.02.2014, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at his correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused has deliberately and wilfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the complainant examined himself on affidavit and additional evidence by way of affidavit and placed on record Power of Attorney is Ex. CW-1/1; Cheque in question is Ex. CW-1/2, Return memo is Ex. CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 4 of 16 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:25:24 +0530 CW-1/3 and Ex. CW-1/4, Copy of legal demand notice and postal receipt Ex. CW-1/5 (Colly) & Ex. CW-1/6 (Colly); Tracking Report Ex. CW-1/7 (Colly); Complaint is Ex. CW-1/8. Photocopy of agreement between complainant and Sh. Yad Ram Ex. CW1/9 (Colly). 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused person was summoned. 5. Upon the appearance of the accused, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon him on 18.11.2014 to which he pleaded not guilty. The accused has accepted issuance of cheque in favour of the complainant and also his signatures on the cheque in question. The accused has denied receiving the legal demand notice. The accused has stated that he did not know the complainant and did not have any transaction or property transaction with the complainant ever. The accused further stated that he knew one Rajender Kumar from whom he had taken a loan of Rs. 50,000/- and handed over a blank signed cheque and a power of attorney of one property of his wife to him as security, but he returned the loan amount to Rajender Kumar and despite requests and demand, Rajender Kumar did not return either the said cheque or the power of attorney. The accused further stated that later both Rajender Kumar and complainant in connivance with each other filled up the particulars of the cheque and filed this false a frivolous case against him. 6. Vide a separate statement of the accused person, the admissions and denials u/s 294 CrPC was recorded. 7. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged on 14.08.2015. CW-2 and CW-3 were examined, cross examined and discharged. CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 5 of 16 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.13 17:25:32 +0530 Thereby, CE was closed. Accordingly, the matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused. 8. Statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC was recorded on 17.05.2022 wherein the accused opted to lead defence evidence. DW 1 Sh. Arvind Kumar was examined, cross examined and discharged on 13.02.2023 and vide order of this court, DE was closed on 14.11.2025. 9. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 10. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 6 of 16 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:25:37 +0530 V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. 11. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 7 of 16 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:25:43 +0530 IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 12. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheque, i.e. Ex. CW1/2. In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has admitted that the cheque in dispute belongs to his company and his signatures on the same. It is also not disputed that the cheque in question is not drawn on the account maintained by the accused person and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheque. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 13. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheque in question was returned vide return memos dated 30.12.2013 & 15.01.2014 (Ex. CW1/3 & Ex. CW1/4) & respectively, due to the reason "Funds Insufficient." By CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 8 of 16 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:25:52 +0530 implication thereof, the cheque was presented within three months and the same was returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 14. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 05.02.2014 (Ex. CW1/5 (Colly)) was dispatched vide Speed Post (Ex. CW1/6 (Colly)), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has accepted the receiving of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. Further, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 15. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 16. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 9 of 16 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:25:58 +0530 cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 17. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 10 of 16 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:26:04 +0530 (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 18. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 19. In the present case, the primary defence of the accused person is that he does not know the complainant and he did not have any property transaction with the complainant. During the cross examination of the complainant as CW1, when he was specifically asked whether any document was executed regarding the transaction, the complainant has stated that no document was executed. During the cross examination, the Ld. Counsel for the accused has questioned the financial capacity of the complainant. As far as the financial capacity of the complainant is concerned, it is a settled position of law that showcasing that complainant did not have adequate financial capacity to lend money to the accused amounts to a probable defence and can help in rebutting the presumption that is accrued to the benefit of the complainant in cheque dishonour cases. 20. In APS Forex Service Private Limited vs Shakti International Fashion Linkers , AIR 2020 SC 945, the Hon'ble Apex Court observed that: - CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 11 of 16 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:26:09 +0530 "When the proceedings were initiated under Section 138 of the N.I. Act the accused denied the debt liability and the accused raised the defence and questioned the financial capacity of the complainant. To that, the complainant failed to prove and establish his financial capacity. Therefore, this Court was satisfied that the accused had a probable defence and consequently in absence of complainant having failed to prove his financial capacity, this Court acquitted the accused. In the present case, the accused never questioned the financial capacity of the complainant. We are of the view that whenever the accused has questioned the financial capacity of the complainant in support of his probable defence, despite the presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act about the presumption of legally enforceable debt and such presumption is rebuttable, thereafter the onus shifts again on the complainant to prove his financial capacity and at that stage the complainant is required to lead the evidence to prove his financial capacity, more particularly when it is a case of giving loan by cash and thereafter issuance of a cheque." 21. Therefore, in cases in which the impugned transaction is in cash, the accused can raise a probable defence by questioning the financial capacity of the complainant, and once the said question is raised, the onus shifts on the complainant to prove his CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 12 of 16 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:26:15 +0530 financial capacity. In the present case, the complainant during his cross examination as CW1 has stated that the sum of Rs. 22,00,000/- was lying at his disposal in his office. In the additional affidavit of the complainant which is Ex. CW1/B, the complainant has stated that he took Rs. 3,75,000/- from CW2 Sh. Rajender Kumar on 08.10.2013 and Rs. 1,00,000/- from Sh. Bhupendra Kumar on the same date. As per the case of the complainant, he had given Rs. 22,00,000/- to the accused on 08.10.2013. Clearly, the complainant took a contradictory stance in the abovementioned statements. 22. The main source of funds for the impugned transaction as per the complainant is the sale transaction with Mr. Yad Ram, the proof of the same is Ex. CW1/9 (Colly). At this stage it is pertinent to mention that Ex. CW1/9 (Colly) are not original documents. The Ld. Counsel for the accused during the cross examination of complainant as CW1 has given a suggestion that it is a forged document. The burden of proving Ex. CW1/9 (Colly) was on the complainant when the genuinity of the same had been disputed. The complainant had failed to examine any witness to the agreement or the second party to the agreement Mr. Yad Ram to prove Ex. CW1/9 (Colly). Therefore, in the absence of the original document or any witness to the execution the Ex. CW1/9 (Colly), the photocopies cannot be relied upon. 23. Further in the additional affidavit of the complainant which is Ex. CW1/B, the complainant has stated that: A. He took Rs. 3,75,000/- from CW2 Sh. Rajender Kumar on 08.10.2013. CW2 during his cross examination has stated that the above said amount was funded by obtaining Rs. 2,00,000/- from the department as loan and Rs. 1,75,000/- were CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 13 of 16 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:26:21 +0530 withdrawn by him. There is no proof of the alleged transaction between the complainant and CW2, as no document was executed. The testimony of CW2 seems very far-fetched because no prudent person would take a loan from his own department to give the same as a loan to some other person. Further the withdrawal of Rs. 1,75,000/- is dated 05.07.2013 and the impugned transaction is dated 08.10.2013. The cash withdrawn by CW2 in the month of July is stated to be given to the complainant as loan in October, the statement of CW2 appears to be flimsy and cannot be relied upon. It appears that the witness has deposed only to support the case of the complainant. B. He took Rs. 1,00,000/- from Sh. Bhupendra Kumar on 08.10.2013. CW3 has stated that the above said amount was withdrawn by him in two transactions of Rs. 49,000/- each dated 16.02.2013. There is no proof of the alleged transaction between the complainant and CW3, as no document was executed. The cash withdrawn by CW3 in the month of February is stated to be given to the complainant as loan in October, the statement of CW2 appears to be flimsy and cannot be relied upon. It appears that the witness has deposed only to support the case of the complainant. C. The complainant in his complaint and evidence by way of affidavit has stated that he had taken Rs. 25,000/- from the market against heavy interest. The complainant has not produced any evidence to prove this transaction as well. 24. The complainant has failed to discharge the burden of showing his financial capacity for the impugned transaction. Per contra the defence of the accused has been consistent in the reply to the legal demand notice which is Ex. CW1/D1, his defence CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 14 of 16 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:26:28 +0530 taken during framing of notice under Section 251 of CrPC and his statement under Section 313 of CrPC. 25. The complainant in his evidence affidavit at paragraph number 12 has stated that the accused had issued the cheque in question. A bare reading of the above said paragraph gives an impression that the complainant is saying that the cheque was filled by the accused and given to him. The accused has stated that the cheque in question was given to Sh. Rajender Kumar as security for a loan of Rs. 50,000/-. Prima facie perusal of the cheque in question, Ex. CW1/2, it is evident that the name of the payee, the amount in digits and words and the date of the issuance of the cheque are not filled by the same person who has signed the cheque in question; as the same are apparently in different ink and prima facie the handwriting also differs. Therefore, the stance taken by the accused appears to be more reliable. 26. In the case of Kulvinder Singh vs Kafeel Ahmad, Crl L. P. 478 of 2011 , decided on 04.01.2013, Hon'ble Delhi High Court has held that the basic principle in criminal law is that the guilt of the accused / respondent must be proved beyond reasonable doubts and if there is any slightest doubt about the commission of an offence, then the benefit has to accrue to him. At the same time, it is important to underscore the established canon of criminal law that in order to pass a conviction in a criminal case, the accused "must be" guilty and not merely "may be" guilty. The mental distance between "may be" guilty to "must be" guilty is a long one and must travel not on surmises and conjectures, but by cogent evidence. Conclusion: 27. In view of the aforesaid discussion, the accused has been successful in CC No. 614535/2016 Mohd. Tufail Vs. Arvind Kumar Jha & Ors. Page 15 of 16 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.13 17:26:33 +0530 establishing a probable defence on a standard of preponderance of probabilities to rebut the presumption under section 118 and 139 of the NI Act by punching the holes in the case of the complainant and making the case of the complainant doubtful. The accused has been successful in establishing a probable defence by way of pointing out the material inconsistencies in the case of the complainant. In the result of the analysis of the present case, the accused Sh. Arvind Kumar Jha, S/o Sh. Radhey Shyam Jha, is hereby acquitted of the offence punishable under Section 138 , Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
